question: Tell me about Matt's leadership journey
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt’s leadership journey grew from delivery teams to building an organization.

Matt’s career progressed from Software Engineer to Solution Architect, Director, and Cloud Innovation Center Leader. His work at **Accenture**, from March **2005** to September **2023**, spanned Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement.

Early management responsibilities centered on delivery: staffing blended onshore/offshore teams, directing work, and handling performance within project timelines. He managed a **40+ person** **JP Morgan Chase** payment-engine and gateway team, along with delivery teams at **Level 3 Communications** and **AT&T**.

The job changed shape when Matt built **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers in Atlanta and Tampa. Clients wanted to move from waterfall and siloed teams to iterative, customer-centric product development. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native experience. Matt became responsible not just for delivery, but for hiring, development, evaluation, promotion, compensation, and remediation, alongside full P&L accountability.

He kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11 to 13** practice and client leads reporting directly to him. Balanced teams combined product, engineering, and design. He introduced pair programming, test-driven development, continuous delivery, and structured “I do, we do, you do” learning. Senior engineers mentored junior practitioners, while weekly tech talks, peer-led demos, and live client projects supported continued learning.

Matt made the final hiring decision on every offer. Because managers did not sit beside practitioners on daily teams, he built evaluations around evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors, rather than visibility to a boss.

The centers grew from **0 to **150+ practitioner**s**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Across **30+ product engagements** and **15+ Fortune **500 client**s**, the practice achieved **4X faster velocity**, zero-defect deployments, and **\$100M+ in repeatable business** through delivery excellence and client relationships.

Matt is currently on sabbatical, building MattGPT and seeking a role where building the product engineering organization, establishing the culture, and delivering results are part of the same job.

question: How does Matt approach complex problems?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt tackles the messy problems.

Matt starts with the people, then the problem. In his work at **Accenture**, that has meant poorly defined problems, stakeholders who disagree, and organizations that may not be ready for change. He listens to understand the business context, the impacts, and the politics before proposing a solution.

He brings technology, product, and business people together to ask: what do they think they’re actually solving? They define a hypothesis, prove or disprove it, and fail fast if needed. Then he helps build the solution design, roadmap, backlog, and plan, with the team owning execution. Regular checkpoints keep tradeoffs visible.

At **Norfolk Southern**, defects were rising even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The client and **Accenture** account leadership raised concerns while the team was also moving to fully remote work during the pandemic. Instead of defending the metrics, Matt took ownership and ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite.

The audit found an engineer writing tests after the code and working from his own interpretation of requirements. Backlog stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done. Matt showed those gaps openly, rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, and brought frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile rituals to bring stakeholders, developers, and product managers together.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Defect rates dropped, and client confidence returned through transparency and visible improvement.

For MattGPT, Matt addressed context loss and unreliable AI-generated changes with persistent working agreements, architectural decision records, session handoffs, and behavior-first tests. He shipped a working product containing **100+ stories**, with eval-driven checks preventing AI-generated regressions from reaching production.

question: What's Matt's leadership philosophy?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” Engineers, designers, and product teams were dealing with role silos, slow handoffs, and environments where fear of blame kept people from experimenting or speaking honestly.

He works to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, build psychological safety, and push decisions to the people closest to the work. He uses transparency, direct feedback, and open communication, and coaches teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. His own phrase is “Builder’s mindset, coach’s heart.”

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, his “permit to fail” culture included non-punitive post-mortems, transparent sharing of errors, and lean, low-stakes experiments. Instead of pointing fingers, teams identified lessons and applied them to subsequent sprints. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used user research and rapid testing to validate assumptions before committing to costly builds, treating failed experiments as decision inputs rather than setbacks.

He also assembled balanced teams with engineers, product managers, and UX architects, with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions replaced isolated work and reduced handoffs. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, lean product and modern engineering practices produced **4x delivery acceleration**. The balanced-team work reduced project delays, improved team satisfaction and retention, and achieved **zero-defect production code**. Matt’s stated non-negotiables include integrity and respect, clarity of purpose, continuous learning, and a focus on outcomes rather than optics.

question: What did Matt learn about risk ownership?
answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

Matt learned that “assumptions are risks in disguise” and that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.”

On a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client, Matt was the tech lead across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation rather than verifying it. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer data had been masked, or implement compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. Communications went to **thousands of real clients**. Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described this as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His lesson was not simply to tell testers to be more careful: IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

In his later team practices, Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. He also placed high-risk, high-complexity work in earlier sprints, with periodic reassessment rather than waiting for late-stage surprises.

question: Why is early failure important?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt put early failure to work.

In **Accenture’s** innovation and product incubation work, teams often arrived expecting polished requirements, predictable outcomes, and linear delivery. But early-stage product development started with assumptions, not certainty. Matt’s goal wasn’t to be right on the first try. It was to reduce risk quickly and cheaply before teams committed to costly builds.

He set expectations upfront that early prototypes, experiments, and user tests would likely fail, and that this was intentional. He used user research, Jobs to Be Done framing, and rapid testing to surface mismatches between assumptions and real user needs. Each test outcome became evidence for shaping the product direction week by week. He also drew a parallel to test-driven development: the first step is supposed to fail because that failure exposes what needs to be built.

That required changing how teams responded to mistakes. At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, fear of blame had led teams to avoid risks, slowing delivery and limiting experimentation. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Teams applied the lessons to subsequent sprints rather than pointing fingers.

The reported outcomes were reduced wasted engineering effort, faster convergence on validated solutions, and shorter project timelines. Early failure eliminated wrong directions before engineering investment. Failed experiments became decision inputs rather than setbacks, and post-mortem learnings prevented identified failure patterns from recurring.

question: What did Matt learn about sustainable leadership?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt learned.

For years at **Accenture**, Matt operated at an unsustainable pace: leading a **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center, driving growth targets, managing client delivery, and developing people. He was proud of the results, but he wasn’t paying attention to the cost. His work-life balance was off, and he didn’t have the boundaries needed to sustain that intensity over time.

After his chapter at **Accenture** ended, he had space to get honest about overcommitment, saying yes to everything, and letting others control his calendar. His lesson was explicit: “Sustainable impact matters more than heroic effort.” He redefined boundaries and self-care as leadership disciplines, not weaknesses, and prioritized health, recovery, and focus as non-negotiables. He committed to building teams where sustainable pace is expected, not exceptional.

His delivery-rhythm work addressed the team side of that problem. When mounting workloads and unpredictable workflows led to extended hours and diminished morale, Matt introduced focused morning stand-ups to agree on goals and blockers, pairing blocks for shared ownership, uninterrupted deep-work sessions, flexible midday recharge breaks, and end-of-day wrap-ups. Teams consistently met daily objectives with minimal overtime; surveys reported improved morale and reduced stress, while burnout declined and retention improved.

He also learned that designing autonomy was not the same as living it. Practitioners accustomed to command-and-control delivery kept pushing decisions upward. Matt repeatedly reinforced shared decision-making across product managers, designers, and engineers, with team leads removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes.

Matt now looks for environments where intensity is balanced with humanity. His stated commitments include boundaries he can articulate and protect, care for himself as well as his teams, and modeling a sustainable pace.

question: Tell me about Matt's payments work at JPMorgan
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

The bank was building ACCESS Next Generation, its global corporate banking portal, on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Its **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries needed payment capabilities beyond the out-of-box offering. Regional systems had different formats, client configurations, and compliance requirements. Corporate treasurers worked across separate local logins, while administrators spent days manually configuring user permissions.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, managing where native platform capabilities ended and custom engineering was required.

Matt designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules. The work included NACHA file validation, foreign exchange integration, payment-type-specific permissions, and Message Authentication Code security so corporate users could verify payment integrity before release. He also built contextual help explaining wire fields, tax codes, and cross-border requirements.

Alongside the payment engine, he delivered a centralized gateway handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12** countries. He led legacy payment data migration without disruption to live payment operations, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability.

For administrators, Matt replaced individual permission configuration with role-based profiles, bulk changes, and a centralized dashboard. Entitlement management dropped from **days to minutes**. He also coordinated jurisdiction-specific data visibility and access controls with regional compliance teams, sequencing launches by regulatory readiness rather than a single global deployment.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for payments across regions, real-time visibility into cash positions, and single sign-on across treasury functions. Matt also owned production incident response, including root-cause analysis and live status communications across bank, offshore, and vendor teams.

question: Tell me about a time Matt failed
answer_md:
Matt’s failure story comes from a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. He was the tech lead, responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles. He relied on inherited documentation and assumed the IAM controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations were correct rather than verifying them.

That assumption had a direct consequence: an offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT that sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. Customer names and email addresses had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

Matt had focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He had not audited who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verified the data masking, or implemented compensating controls such as email interception. After the incident, he took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described this as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His account places responsibility on the environment he was supposed to verify, not simply on the tester who triggered the job.

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His phrase for the lesson was: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”

question: What makes your approach to TDD different?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt put test-first into practice.

Enterprise teams were writing code quickly, discovering defects weeks later, and spending weeks debugging. Developers could build technically correct code that still missed business intent because development and acceptance criteria lived in separate worlds. Clients questioned paying for **two** engineers at **one** keyboard; traditional delivery teams saw pairing as inefficient and TDD as overhead. At **Norfolk Southern**, even after a quality crisis was contained, the question remained: would the practices hold after the TDD experts went home?

Matt established an “outside-in” development cycle rather than treating TDD as unit-test coverage alone. Every feature began with BDD acceptance criteria in Gherkin, Given/When/Then, before production code. Product owners, developers, and QA used the same living specification. Acceptance tests defined the outer boundary, integration tests connected behavior to components, and Red-Green-Refactor drove implementation: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then safely refactor. A feature was not done until both unit tests and acceptance criteria passed.

He adapted the discipline to existing tools, including Cucumber, Cypress, Tosca, and Jasmine, rather than requiring a framework change. Tests ran in CI/CD and blocked merges when they failed. New features required tests; bugs required regression tests.

Adoption meant showing and doing, not just mandating compliance. Matt paired experienced practitioners with newer developers, rotated partners, and used retrospectives to adjust pairing. At **Norfolk Southern**, test cases became a discrete step before the solution, checked at standup. Stories were capped at **three points** for **one-week** iterations, and remote pairs traded drivers frequently.

Across the enterprise engagements, teams reached **4X velocity** compared with client internal teams after the learning curve. At **Capital One**, the **eight-person** team delivered features **3 to **4x** faster** than other **Accenture** teams on that engagement, with **zero production defects**. Matt applies the behavior-first discipline to MattGPT too, with **43 passing BDD scenarios** across its API, business logic, and UI.

question: How did Matt modernize payments across 12+ countries at JP Morgan?

Alongside the gateway, he delivered bespoke payment modules, payment verification controls, and payment-type-specific permissions. Bulk permission changes reduced entitlement management from days to minutes.

The rollout also required migrating client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories without disrupting live payments. Matt introduced compliance dashboards and mapped jurisdiction-specific requirements into data visibility and access controls. Regional launches were sequenced by regulatory readiness rather than a single global deployment. He also owned production incident response across releases and migrations.

The Integrated Global Payments Interface launched in **April 2011**, giving corporate treasurers a single entry point for Wire, ACH, and Cross-Border Transfers across **12 countries**. The broader ACCESS portal consolidated regional systems for **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**, with uninterrupted payment operations during migration.

question: Tell me about Matt's early failure and experimentation approach
answer_md:

A container-breach demonstration sent a live alert to a visiting client’s own phone, giving the client working evidence rather than a slide deck.

Teams reduced wasted engineering effort by eliminating wrong directions before costly builds. Post-mortem lessons informed subsequent sprints, preventing repeat failure patterns. Liquid Studio delivered functional solutions in **days, not weeks**, while hypothesis-driven design produced validated MVPs faster with fewer change requests and less rework.

question: What did Matt learn about risk ownership?
answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

Matt learned that “assumptions are risks in disguise” and that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.”

He was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt relied on that documentation rather than verifying the controls himself.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients. Matt had not audited who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirmed that customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implemented compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” which reinforced his belief that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

The change in his delivery approach was explicit: IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became “day-one leadership responsibilities.” Rather than inheriting assurances that an environment was safe, Matt made verifying those assumptions part of the work he was responsible for.

question: Why is early failure important?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt used early failure in product development.

At **Accenture**, teams often entered innovation engagements expecting polished requirements, predictable outcomes, and linear delivery. But early-stage product development had assumptions, not certainty. Waiting to test those assumptions meant committing engineering effort before knowing whether the product addressed real user needs. In the Cloud Innovation Center, fear of blame also discouraged experimentation, contributing to stagnation and slower delivery.

Matt set expectations upfront that early prototypes, experiments, and user tests would likely fail, and that this was intentional. The goal wasn’t to be right on the first try: it was to reduce risk quickly and cheaply. He used user research, Jobs to Be Done (JTBD) framing, and rapid testing to surface mismatches between assumptions and real user needs. He drew parallels to TDD: the first step is supposed to fail because that failure exposes what needs to be built.

Instead of treating failed experiments as setbacks, teams used them as decision inputs and shaped product direction week by week. Matt supported lean, low-stakes experiments and non-punitive post-mortems. Teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints, preventing recurrence of identified failure patterns. They reduced wasted engineering effort and converged on validated solutions faster.

That safety net was not permission to leave operational risks unchecked. In one financial-services engagement, unverified environment controls allowed a UAT email job to send unmasked production data to thousands of real clients. Matt took accountability and led root cause analysis and remediation.

While building MattGPT, he made verification part of development through small, testable increments, behavior-first tests, and eval suites. When a cleanup filter failed to stop unwanted chatbot language, he investigated conflicting prompt instructions rather than adding another patch. Those checks caught AI-generated regressions before production.

question: Tell me about a time Matt failed
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed by relying on assumptions instead of verifying the controls his team depended on.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verify that production customer data had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand the insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and unscrubbed production data, then implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Following the incident, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His stated lesson was that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.”

question: Tell me about Matt's early failure and experimentation approach
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt approached early failure and experimentation.

In **Accenture’s** innovation and product incubation work, teams often arrived expecting polished requirements, predictable outcomes, and linear delivery. Instead, they had assumptions, not answers. At the Cloud Innovation Center, fear of blame also kept some teams from taking risks, slowing delivery and preventing them from trying new engineering practices.

Matt set expectations upfront that early prototypes, experiments, and user tests would likely fail, and that this was intentional. The goal wasn’t to be right on the first try. It was to reduce risk quickly and cheaply before committing to costly builds.

He used user research, Jobs-to-be-Done framing, and rapid testing to find mismatches between assumptions and real user needs. Product managers, designers, and engineers defined hypotheses and testing criteria together, then tested mockups and wireframes with users. Every outcome became evidence for the next iteration. Matt drew a parallel to TDD: the first step is supposed to fail because that failure exposes what needs to be built.

He also organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasizing lessons rather than pointing fingers. Teams applied those lessons in subsequent sprints, preventing repeated failure patterns. They began experimenting more freely, eliminated wrong product directions before engineering investment, and delivered validated MVPs faster with fewer change requests and less rework.

That “permit to fail” did not mean leaving operational risks unchecked. In a separate financial-services engagement, an offshore tester triggered a UAT email job containing unmasked production data, reaching thousands of real clients. Matt took accountability and led root cause analysis and remediation. IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one responsibilities.

He continued testing and diagnosing failures while building MattGPT. When a language filter failed, he traced conflicting prompt instructions rather than adding another patch. After rebuilding the prompt structure, eval-suite failures dropped from **32.3%** to roughly **3% to 6%**.

question: What makes your approach to TDD different?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt approaches TDD.

Enterprise teams were writing code quickly, discovering defects late, and spending weeks debugging. The problem went beyond unit-test coverage: developers could build technically correct code that still failed to meet business intent. Clients questioned paying for **two** engineers at **one** keyboard, while delivery teams saw pairing as inefficient and TDD as overhead.

Matt established an “outside-in” development cycle rather than treating TDD as an isolated unit-testing practice. Every feature began with BDD acceptance criteria in Gherkin, Given/When/Then, before production code. Product owners, developers, and QA shared the same executable specification. Acceptance tests defined the outer boundary, integration tests connected behavior to components, and Red-Green-Refactor drove implementation: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then safely refactor. A feature was not done until both unit tests and acceptance criteria passed.

He adapted that discipline to existing toolchains, including Cucumber, Cypress, Tosca, and Jasmine. Tests became CI/CD merge gates; bugs required regression tests. At the Cloud Innovation Center, he paired experienced developers with newer engineers, rotated partners, and used retrospectives to adjust pairing.

At **Norfolk Southern**, a quality crisis exposed that having practices in place was not enough. Matt made test-case creation a discrete step before engineering the solution, checked at standup. Pairs rotated daily, and stories entered sprints only when testable and small enough for a **one-week** iteration. The practices held after outside experts left; the crisis failure mode did not recur.

At **Capital One**, disciplined TDD/BDD against a client-prioritized backlog delivered features **3 to 4x** faster than other **Accenture** teams on that engagement, with **zero production defects**. Matt applies the same behavior-first discipline to MattGPT, where **43** passing BDD scenarios cover cross-layer behavior, not just individual components.

question: How does Matt approach complex problems?

question: What did Matt learn about risk ownership?
answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

Matt learned that “assumptions are risks in disguise” and that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.”

On a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client, Matt was the tech lead responsible for a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt relied on the existing documentation rather than verifying that those controls were correct.

He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or confirm that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments. An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT, sending communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described this as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” That consequence reinforced his belief that leaders own the environment, rather than leaving individuals to bear the consequences of controls that leadership had not verified.

IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. In his Cloud Innovation Center work at **Accenture**, he also organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments, with lessons applied to subsequent sprints to prevent recurrence of identified failure patterns.

question: Tell me about Matt's payments work at JPMorgan
answer_md:
🐾 Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase** centered on building ACCESS Next Generation, its unified global corporate banking portal.

The bank was consolidating regional treasury and payment systems, but Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform did not cover its requirements out of the box. Each payment type had different formatting, validation, compliance, and approval workflows. Connectivity across **12 countries** involved different protocols and payment schemes, while legacy user permissions took days of manual configuration. The global rollout also had to accommodate conflicting regional rules for data visibility and access.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, determining where native platform capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. That included validating NACHA output, integrating the bank’s foreign exchange engine, and implementing Message Authentication Code security so corporate users could verify payment integrity before release. He also built the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing to internal settlement and compliance systems and external payment rails.

For administration, Matt replaced individual permission configuration with role-based profiles and bulk changes across users, accounts, and products. Payment-specific controls could authorize wire approval without permitting FX initiation. Entitlement management dropped from days to minutes.

He led legacy payment data migration without disruption to live payment operations, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. question: Tell me about a time Matt failed
answer_md:
Matt’s failure was assuming that security controls were correct rather than verifying them. He was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client, with dev, QA, UAT, and production environments. The program was under delivery pressure, and offshore teams were executing test cycles using environment configurations and documentation inherited from earlier phases.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not validate IAM configuration and downstream access controls, audit who could trigger email processes, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

For development, Matt moved from ChatGPT to Claude and Claude Code, using Gemini situationally. He established persistent working agreements, session handoffs, Architecture Decision Records, golden-query evaluations, and behavior-first tests instead of relying on “just chat and hope.”

The shipped MVP includes semantic search across **100+ stories**, a conversational interface, and source citations. Matt built it as a solo developer, with eval-driven checks and behavior-first tests preventing AI-generated regressions from reaching production.

question: What makes your approach to TDD different?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt put TDD into practice.

Matt’s approach started with a problem broader than unit test coverage: developers were building technically correct code that still failed to meet business intent. QA discovered problems weeks later, when context was lost and fixes were expensive. Clients questioned paying for **two** engineers at **one** keyboard, while delivery teams saw pairing as inefficient and TDD as overhead.

Instead of treating TDD as an isolated developer practice, Matt established an “outside-in” development cycle. Every feature began with BDD acceptance criteria in Gherkin (Given/When/Then), before production code. Product owners, developers, and QA worked from the same living specification. Acceptance tests defined the outer boundary, integration tests connected behavior to components, and Red-Green-Refactor drove implementation: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then safely refactor. A feature was not done until unit tests and BDD acceptance criteria both passed.

Matt reinforced that workflow through hands-on pairing, not just training or mandates. At **Norfolk Southern**, after a quality crisis, building test cases became a discrete step before engineering the solution, inside a pair and checked at standup. Pairs rotated daily; newer engineers worked beside seasoned practitioners. Stories entered sprints only when discrete and testable. In the Cloud Innovation Center, retrospectives also informed adjustments to pairing frequency and work-style clashes. Tests ran in CI/CD, preventing merges unless every level passed; bugs required regression tests.

The discipline accommodated existing tools, including Cucumber, Cypress, Tosca, and Jasmine, rather than requiring a framework change alongside a practice change. Matt continues the behavior-first practice in MattGPT, where **43** passing BDD scenarios cover cross-layer behavior using pytest-bdd and Playwright.

At **Capital One**, disciplined TDD/BDD and a value-prioritized backlog delivered features **3-4x** faster than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**. At **JP Morgan Chase**, Gherkin scenarios served as the acceptance criteria for a mobile banking platform with full Product Owner sign-off. At **Norfolk Southern**, pairing and test-first remained the default after outside experts left.

question: How does Matt approach complex problems?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt tackles the messy problems.

Matt starts with the people, then the problem. His work has included poorly defined issues, conflicting priorities, and organizations that weren’t ready for change. His starting point is that teams can fail because they’re solving the wrong problem, not because they can’t execute.

He listens to understand the business context, impacts, and politics. Then he brings technology, product, and business participants together to define a hypothesis: what do they think they’re actually solving? He works to prove or disprove it before committing to a solution. From there, he builds the solution design, roadmap, backlog, and plan, with regular checkpoints and visible tradeoffs. The team owns execution.

At **Norfolk Southern**, that meant questioning reassuring metrics. The team was also moving to fully remote work during the pandemic. Instead of defending the dashboard, Matt took ownership in front of the client and **Accenture** account leadership and ran a bottom-up audit.

He found an engineer interpreting requirements independently and writing tests after the code. Vague backlog stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done. Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts alongside the engineers. Coaching included coding katas, practice sessions, and an “I do, we do, you do” progression. Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

While building MattGPT, he applied hypothesis and verification to AI-assisted development rather than “just chat and hope.” He used persistent working agreements, session handoffs, Architecture Decision Records, behavior-first tests, and small, testable increments. Those practices reduced repeated context explanation and prevented AI-generated regressions from reaching production. He shipped a working product with **100+ stories**, RAG architecture, and a polished UI as a solo developer.

question: What did Matt learn about risk ownership?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the incident behind that lesson.

Matt learned that “assumptions are risks in disguise” and that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.” On a global platform modernization for a financial services client, he was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production. Under delivery pressure, he relied on inherited documentation rather than verifying IAM configuration, environment boundaries, and downstream access controls.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients. Matt had not audited who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verified whether customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implemented compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described this as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” That consequence reinforced his belief that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

In his delivery approach, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities. Rather than treating inherited documentation as confirmation that controls were correct, Matt’s lesson was to verify those controls himself.

question: Tell me about a time Matt failed
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed on a platform delivery.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on the existing documentation rather than verifying it.

He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

question: Tell me about Matt's early failure and experimentation approach

question: What makes your approach to TDD different?
answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt’s approach starts with business behavior, not unit-test coverage alone.

Enterprise teams were writing code quickly, discovering defects weeks later, and spending weeks debugging. Developers could build technically correct code that still missed business intent because acceptance criteria and implementation lived in separate worlds. Clients questioned paying for **two** engineers at **one** keyboard; delivery teams saw pairing as inefficient and TDD as overhead.

Matt established an “outside-in” development cycle. Before production code, product owners, developers, and QA defined BDD acceptance criteria in Gherkin: Given/When/Then. Those scenarios became a shared, executable specification, not a separate requirements document. BDD defined the outer boundary, integration tests connected behavior to system components, and TDD drove implementation through Red-Green-Refactor: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then safely refactor. A feature was not done until unit tests and BDD acceptance criteria both passed.

He taught the discipline through hands-on workshops and paired experienced practitioners with developers new to TDD, rather than relying on mandates. At the Cloud Innovation Center, pairing included role rotation and retrospectives to adjust pairing frequency and address work-style clashes. Teams retained their existing testing ecosystems, including Cucumber, Cypress, Tosca, and Jasmine. CI/CD blocked merges unless tests passed; new features required tests, and bugs required regression tests.

At **Norfolk Southern**, a quality crisis showed that introducing practices was not enough. Matt rebuilt the daily workflow so test cases were a discrete step before the solution, checked at standup. Pairs rotated daily, and newer engineers worked beside seasoned practitioners. The practices held after outside experts left, and the crisis failure mode did not recur.

At **Capital One**, the team delivered features **3-**4x** faster** than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**. At **JP Morgan**, Gherkin scenarios served as acceptance criteria for a mobile banking platform with full Product Owner sign-off. Matt applies the same behavior-first discipline to MattGPT, with **43 passing BDD scenarios** across its application layers.

question: Tell me about the CIC

Product, design, and engineering worked in silos, with handoffs between functions. **Accenture** had piloted the CIC model in Columbus; Matt’s task was to expand it while adapting startup practices for enterprise compliance, security, and legacy complexity.

He created collaborative workspaces with pairing stations, whiteboards, and client co-location spaces. Balanced teams brought product managers, designers, and engineers together. Instead of requirements-driven feature delivery and a separate QA phase, teams used customer journey-led development, pair programming, test-driven development, and automated deployment pipelines.

Many recruits lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Prospective clients experienced the work firsthand rather than hearing a methodology presentation. A skeptical railroad client visited the Atlanta center and watched standups and collaborative problem-solving. Matt also connected clients and practitioners with Georgia Tech research, startups, hackathons, and recruiting. Separately, at **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, his TICARA toolkit reduced cloud environment setup from days to under an hour.

The Atlanta and Tampa CICs grew from zero to **150+ practitioners**, delivering **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune **500 client**s**. Results included **4X faster velocity**, zero-defect deployments, and **10-person** teams delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams. question: How did Matt handle failure?
answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt handled failure, including an incident he took accountability for.

In one global financial services platform modernization engagement, Matt was the tech lead across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. Under delivery pressure, he relied on inherited documentation rather than verifying IAM controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access. He also did not confirm that production customer data had been masked or scrubbed.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT that sent communications containing unmasked production data to **thousands of real clients**. Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation, working collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded the tester’s removal: “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities.

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, teams had avoided risks because they feared blame, slowing delivery and experimentation. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than pointing fingers, and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Teams applied post-mortem findings in subsequent sprints, preventing recurrence of identified failure patterns and shortening project timelines.

In product incubation, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. He used user research, JTBD framing, and rapid testing to uncover mismatches between assumptions and real user needs before costly builds. Failed experiments became decision inputs rather than setbacks.

While building MattGPT, Matt also addressed failures in his own development process. When a chatbot filter failed to stop evaluative language, he traced the problem to conflicting prompt instructions rather than expanding the ban list. Rebuilding the prompt reduced eval-suite failures from **32.3%** to roughly **3 to 6%**. For AI-assisted development more broadly, he added persistent working agreements, session handoffs, architecture decision records, eval-driven checks, and behavior-first tests to catch AI-generated regressions before production.
